question:
A regional electric utility's AI steering committee is prioritizing two proposals. One proposal is a supervised model to predict transformer failures from historical maintenance records. Another proposal is a generative AI assistant that summarizes repair manuals, field notes, and email messages. Leaders want realistic expectations about data preparation based on data type and AI approach.

Which TWO actions should the committee recommend?
options: Create high-quality labeled examples for the supervised model so training and assessment have ground truth.
Use SQL queries as the primary analysis method for repair manuals, field notes, and emails because they mention assets.
Require analysts to label every repair manual, field note, and email message before the generative AI effort can start.
Use large unstructured or semi-structured content for the generative AI effort without requiring labels for pre-training.
Classify maintenance notes and email messages as structured data whenever they include dates, asset IDs, or numbers.
explanation:
Data type matters because it influences how much preparation is needed and which AI approach is appropriate. Structured data follows a standardized format or predefined schema, often with rows, columns, field names, data types, and constraints, while unstructured data is not forced into that kind of predefined structure. AWS describes these distinctions in What is Structured Data?.

For a supervised ML use case, AWS explains that the model needs a labeled dataset, and a properly labeled dataset used for training and assessment is called ground truth. The quality of that ground truth affects model accuracy, so a business team should plan for reliable labels when sponsoring a supervised prediction initiative. See What is Data Labeling? for the business-level explanation.

Generative AI has a different data profile. AWS Prescriptive Guidance explains that traditional ML often relies on structured or labeled datasets, while generative AI models can learn from large amounts of unstructured or semi-structured data and do not require explicit labels for pre-training, as described in Differences between traditional machine learning and generative AI. This is why the committee should not treat every document source as requiring manual labels before the generative AI initiative can begin.

question:
A national museum network is expanding AI initiatives for visitor personalization, collection metadata enrichment, donor outreach, and employee knowledge support. The first pilots created disputes about who owns AI readiness capabilities such as workforce training, policy updates, change communications, and business value tracking. The transformation lead wants an accountability model that follows AWS CAF-AI guidance and avoids treating AI adoption as only an engineering responsibility.

Which action should the transformation lead take?
options: Create a temporary review group after deployment. Use post-launch issues to decide which functions need ongoing involvement.
Map each AI adoption capability to shared business and functional owners. Define decision rights, handoffs, and success measures.
Assign each department independent ownership of its AI use cases. Let local managers define controls, handoffs, and success metrics.
Place all AI adoption capabilities under the data science team. Measure progress by model delivery milestones and experiment throughput.
explanation:
AWS CAF-AI frames AI adoption around organizational capabilities across Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security, and Operations. The ownership of these capabilities can vary by organization, and multiple stakeholders often share interest in the same capability, so an effective operating model needs shared ownership with clear decision rights and accountability.

For a transformation program, the practical goal is not to make every group jointly responsible for everything. The goal is to define who contributes expertise, who approves decisions, who escalates unresolved issues, and how business value and responsible use will be measured. This reduces the risk of both extremes: a technology-only program that misses organizational readiness, and a fragmented program where each department invents its own standards.

AWS CAF-AI also emphasizes that AI initiatives depend on collaboration across stakeholders, business units, and practices. For more detail, see Foundational AI capabilities and Governance perspective: Managing an AI/ML-driven organization.

question:
A luxury hotel group's guest experience office piloted an AI concierge that answered common guest questions and reduced call volume. Competitors can quickly copy a similar chatbot. Executives now want AI to produce a durable advantage across loyalty, staffing, and service recovery without turning the effort into a technical deployment project.

Which action should the office recommend?
options: Ask each department to launch separate AI pilots and compare short-term productivity gains.
Expand the concierge chatbot across all hotel brands and measure savings from fewer support contacts.
Select one model architecture for every use case and standardize future AI deployments around it.
Use an AI adoption framework to mature repeatable capabilities and scale beyond isolated pilots.
explanation:
Sustainable advantage from AI usually comes from more than deploying one visible feature. A chatbot can create useful efficiency, but competitors can often copy the same customer-facing capability. A stronger strategic move is to build repeatable AI capabilities, such as consistent ways to identify opportunities, align them to business outcomes, prepare the organization for adoption, and scale beyond isolated pilots.

The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework for Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Generative AI is described as a mental model for organizations that want to generate business value from AI, mature AI and ML capabilities, and move beyond a single proof of concept. AWS also frames AI value broadly, including customer insight, employee efficiency, accelerated innovation, revenue growth, reduced risk, ESG performance, and operational efficiency. For more, see AWS CAF for Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Generative AI and AI cloud transformation value chain.

question:
A consumer electronics manufacturer's industrial design group wants to let designers use generative AI for early product sketches and naming ideas. Legal leaders are concerned that employees could paste supplier drawings, unreleased product details, or licensed brand assets into public AI tools, and that the inputs or outputs could be reused outside company control. Leadership wants to keep experimentation moving while reducing intellectual property exposure.

Which TWO actions should leadership take?
options: Treat all AI-created sketches as company-owned intellectual property after employees save them in the design repository and add a copyright notice.
Allow employees to use public generative AI tools after removing customer names, project codes, and launch dates from prompts.
Rely on a standard prompt instruction that tells each AI tool not to store, reuse, retain, or learn from company inputs.
Use an approved enterprise generative AI service that does not use customer prompts or outputs to train base models.
Establish an acceptable-use policy that restricts confidential source materials to approved generative AI tools.
explanation:
Intellectual property risk in generative AI is not limited to the final image or text. The inputs can contain trade secrets, supplier-owned drawings, licensed assets, or unreleased product plans, and the organization needs governance before employees use those materials in AI tools.

A practical business control is to combine an approved enterprise service with clear usage rules. For example, Data protection in Amazon Bedrock explains that Amazon Bedrock does not use customer prompts or responses to train base models, and model providers do not have access to customer prompts or responses. That type of service-level commitment helps reduce IP exposure compared with uncontrolled use of public tools.

Policies are also necessary because technology choice alone does not tell employees which materials are appropriate to submit. An acceptable-use policy should define approved tools, prohibited source material, and escalation paths for licensed or third-party content. Prompt disclaimers, partial anonymization, and internal storage labels are weak substitutes because they do not change provider terms or resolve ownership and licensing questions.

question:
A city transportation authority is considering AI to improve bus maintenance planning. Leaders have identified several possible tools, but they have not agreed whether success should be measured by technician time saved, fewer service disruptions, lower repair costs, or improved rider satisfaction. Finance needs a credible ROI estimate before approving funding.

Which action should the strategy team take FIRST?
options: Estimate licensing costs for each tool and treat the lowest-cost option as the best ROI.
Adopt a pilot across all teams and report qualitative feedback after the first funding cycle.
Define the business problem, expected value, and observable KPI baseline before estimating returns.
Benchmark available AI tools by feature coverage and choose the option with the broadest capabilities.
explanation:
A credible AI ROI case starts with the business outcome, not with the tool. The team must identify the business problem, the expected business value, and an observable performance metric before estimating whether an AI initiative is worth funding.

For a transportation authority, ROI could include several valid dimensions: technician productivity, avoided repair costs, fewer service disruptions, or improved rider satisfaction. Without selecting and baselining the relevant KPIs, the team cannot compare expected benefits with project costs in a defensible way.

AWS guidance frames AI value broadly across revenue growth, operational efficiency, risk reduction, and other business outcomes. The AWS CAF also emphasizes that AI transformation should begin by identifying and prioritizing opportunities that align to measurable business outcomes. See Your AI transformation journey and Data science.

Tool benchmarking, lowest-cost selection, and broad pilots can all be useful at later stages, but each falls short if the organization has not first defined what value it expects to create. Starting with measurable outcomes gives finance and business leaders a shared basis for comparing time savings, cost reduction, service quality, and other ROI drivers.
